title: Cross-Brand Return Ring with Shared Payment Instrument
scenario:
NetSuite — Returns Dashboard (Brand: UrbanEdge)
Return #RE-20260412: SKU UE-8834 (leather jacket, $389) returned 4/12/2026. Refund issued to Visa ending 4471. Customer: 'David Morales', 118 Flatbush Ave, Brooklyn, NY. Reason: 'Didn't fit.' Store associate: Marcus T. (Location: UrbanEdge SoHo). No receipt — POS lookup matched purchase from 3/28.

NetSuite — Returns Dashboard (Brand: Threads & Co)
Return #TC-20260415: SKU TC-2209 (cashmere wrap, $275) returned 4/15/2026. Refund issued to Visa ending 4471. Customer: 'D. Morales', 118 Flatbush Ave Apt 3, Brooklyn, NY. Reason: 'Defective.' Store associate: Priya K. (Location: Threads & Co Williamsburg).

Shopify — Online Returns (Brand: KineticWear)
RMA #KW-9921: Order KW-5567812, SKU KW-APEX-BLK (running shoes, $210) returned via mail 4/18/2026. Refund to PayPal (david.m.nyc@gmail.com). Shipping label origin: Brooklyn, NY 11217. Customer account: 'DaveMNYC'. Account created 3/15/2026.

Square POS — Exception Report (Brand: UrbanEdge, SoHo location)
Alert: Associate Marcus T. processed 4 refund-without-receipt transactions in 14-day window (threshold: 5/30 days). Individual amounts: $389, $215, $178, $290. All within authority limit ($400).

Slack — #lp-alerts (Apr 19, 2026, 9:47 AM)
@jenny.okafor: Hey @anthony.dimaggio — Riskified flagged a velocity cluster on card ending 4471. Seven purchases across 3 brands in 21 days, all high-value apparel. Six have already been returned. The 7th is a $520 coat from Threads & Co purchased yesterday.
@anthony.dimaggio: Which brands? Do we have a unified customer ID?
@jenny.okafor: No, separate profiles per brand obviously. But the card match is clean. Also the PayPal on the KW return resolves to the same name.
@anthony.dimaggio: Put a return hold on the coat. I'll pull the full picture.
[reacted with: eyes emoji]

Google Sheets — 'LP Exception Log Q2 2026'
Row 34: Date: 4/12 | Brand: UrbanEdge | Flag: 'Refund w/o receipt over $300 — manager override by Sandra L.' | Notes: 'Sandra approved verbally, Marcus processed. Sandra noted customer was VIP loyalty member.' | Policy ref: 'RP-2025-v3 Sec 4.1'

Zendesk — Ticket #ZD-442918 (Brand: KineticWear)
Customer: DaveMNYC | Created: 4/16/2026 | Subject: 'Return label not working'
Agent note (internal, 4/17): 'Customer demanding expedited return. Mentioned he returns frequently and has never had issues. Offered $25 credit to resolve. Customer accepted but still wants full refund on item.'
question: Based on the available evidence, what is the correct next action for Loss Prevention?
choices: A) Escalate Sandra L. for the manager override on the $389 return — the exception log shows she approved a refund-without-receipt over the $300 threshold in RP-2025-v3, which requires LP director sign-off
B) No action needed yet — each individual brand's returns are within policy limits, and the card match alone is insufficient without identity verification across brands
C) Flag Marcus T. for internal investigation — his exception count is approaching threshold and the refund-without-receipt on the $389 jacket is the primary concern

D) Treat this as a confirmed cross-brand ORC pattern tied to a single actor via payment instrument matching, place holds on all pending returns linked to card 4471 and the associated PayPal, and escalate to the multi-brand fraud committee
rationale: The Riskified velocity flag, consistent card-last-4 across two in-store brands, PayPal resolution to the same name, matching address (with slight apartment variation), and the pattern of high-value purchase-then-return across brands within 21 days constitutes a textbook ORC wardrobing pattern. The critical signal in Slack confirms Riskified already linked the activity, and Anthony's own instruction to 'put a return hold' validates this is actionable. Answer A focuses only on the associate (who is a tool, not the actor) and misses the cross-brand pattern. Answer C applies single-brand threshold logic to what is clearly a multi-system synthesis problem — no single brand sees the full picture, which is exactly how these rings operate. Answer D focuses on a policy compliance issue with the manager override, which is a secondary finding, not the primary threat. The entity resolution across brands (name variations, address variation, different systems) is the core challenge that makes B correct.

title: Refund Authority Threshold Change with Undocumented Grace Period
scenario:
Google Workspace — 'Return & Refund Policy RP-2026-v1' (Published Feb 1, 2026)
Section 4.2: 'Refund-without-receipt transactions exceeding $100 require Loss Prevention Manager approval. Store managers may approve refunds without receipt up to $100.'
Section 4.2 (Footnote): 'Replaces RP-2025-v3 Section 4.1, effective immediately upon publication.'

Google Workspace — 'Return & Refund Policy RP-2025-v3' (Archived Jan 31, 2026)
Section 4.1: 'Refund-without-receipt transactions exceeding $300 require LP Director approval. Store managers may approve refunds without receipt up to $300.'

Slack — #store-managers (Feb 1, 2026, 8:02 AM)
@corporate.ops: Team — new return policy RP-2026-v1 is live today. Key change: refund w/o receipt threshold dropped from $300 to $100 for manager-level authority. Please review and confirm.
[14 of 47 managers reacted with checkmark emoji]
[No further replies in thread]

Slack — #store-managers (Feb 3, 2026, 11:15 AM)
@rachel.nguyen: Quick q — I have a customer in-store right now with a $180 return, no receipt. Under the old policy I could approve this. Are we really enforcing the new limit starting today?
@corporate.ops: Policy is effective as of 2/1. Please follow the new threshold.
@sandra.lowell: @rachel.nguyen just call LP, they're turning these around in under 5 min
@rachel.nguyen: Got it, thanks

Slack — DM between Anthony DiMaggio and VP of Retail Ops, Karen Marsh (Feb 1, 2026, 10:22 AM)
@karen.marsh: Anthony — heads up, we're going to get a flood of calls on the new $100 limit. Can you give managers a soft 2-week grace period to adjust? Don't formally flag anyone processing between $100-$300 until Feb 15.
@anthony.dimaggio: Makes sense. I'll tell my team to note but not escalate until the 15th.
@karen.marsh: Perfect. Don't put that in writing anywhere official though — I don't want it as a documented exception.

Square POS — Exception Report (UrbanEdge, 5 locations, Feb 1-14, 2026)
23 refund-without-receipt transactions between $100-$300 approved by store managers during this window. None escalated to LP.

Square POS — Exception Report (UrbanEdge, Midtown location, Feb 18, 2026)
Alert: Manager Sandra L. processed refund-without-receipt for $245. Customer: 'T. Whittaker'. No LP approval on file.

Google Sheets — 'LP Exception Log Q1 2026'
Row 12: Date: 2/18 | Brand: UrbanEdge | Location: Midtown | Flag: 'Refund w/o receipt $245, no LP approval' | Manager: Sandra L. | Status: 'Pending review' | Notes: [empty]

Zendesk — Ticket #ZD-438201 (Feb 18, 2026)
Customer: T. Whittaker | Subject: 'Refund issue in store'
Agent note (internal): 'Customer states manager approved refund but it was reversed the next day. Customer upset. Manager Sandra L. says she thought the old policy still applied.'
question: Sandra L. processed a $245 refund-without-receipt on Feb 18 without LP approval. How should this be adjudicated?
choices: A) Inconclusive — the grace period was never formally documented, creating ambiguity about whether it constitutes a policy modification; escalate to Legal/HR for interpretation before taking action
B) No violation — Sandra's claim that she didn't see the policy update is supported by the fact that only 14 of 47 managers acknowledged the Slack announcement, suggesting insufficient notice

C) Clear policy violation — RP-2026-v1 took effect Feb 1, the published policy requires LP approval over $100, the grace period ended Feb 15, and Sandra processed this transaction on Feb 18; she must be formally flagged

D) No violation — the informal grace period communicated by the VP of Retail Ops via DM to Anthony extends manager authority to $300 through at least Feb 15, and a reasonable interpretation allows additional adjustment time
rationale: The DM between Anthony and Karen Marsh explicitly bounds the grace period to Feb 15 ('Don't formally flag anyone processing between $100-$300 until Feb 15'). Sandra's transaction on Feb 18 falls three days after the grace period expired. While the grace period was informal and undocumented by design (Karen explicitly said 'don't put that in writing'), it had a clear end date that has passed. Answer A incorrectly extends the grace period beyond its stated boundary with a vague 'reasonable interpretation' — the DM is specific about Feb 15. Answer C is tempting because the grace period lacks formal documentation, but Anthony was party to the agreement and knows its terms; from his operational perspective this is clear, not ambiguous. Answer D confuses notification adequacy with policy enforceability — the Slack announcement plus the published policy document constitute sufficient notice under Atlas's change management procedures, and Sandra had 17 days of the policy being live before her transaction. The 23 transactions in the Feb 1-14 window are correctly un-escalated per the informal agreement; Sandra's Feb 18 transaction is not.

Row 52: Date: 3/25 | Brand: Threads & Co | Flag: 'TC-1187 variance' | Status: 'Open' | Notes: blank

Slack — #lp-team (Mar 26, 2026, 2:14 PM)
@jenny.okafor: Weird one. Pulled the refund details on the Fontaine transactions at Herald Sq. All three refunds were processed to prepaid Visa cards. Different card numbers each time.
@anthony.dimaggio: Prepaid cards on refund-without-receipt? That's a red flag. Same for the other locations?
@jenny.okafor: Checking... Tran's refunds went to prepaid Visa too. Washington's went to a regular debit card though.
@jenny.okafor: Oh wait — I just ran the card BINs. Fontaine and Tran's prepaid cards are all from the same issuer batch (BIN 4147-83xx). That's a Walgreens gift card BIN.
@anthony.dimaggio: eyes emoji

Slack — DM between Jenny Okafor and Anthony DiMaggio (Mar 26, 2026, 3:45 PM)
@jenny.okafor: One more thing. I looked up Fontaine, Tran, and Washington on LinkedIn. Fontaine and Tran both previously worked at Nordstrom Rack — same location, overlapping dates. Washington I can't connect yet.
@anthony.dimaggio: Don't put LinkedIn stuff in the official log. Note the card BIN match only for now. I'll request the prepaid card purchase records from Walgreens corporate through our ORC network.

Looker — Refund Pattern Dashboard (filtered Mar 2026)
All refund-without-receipt transactions $85-$100 across all Atlas brands: 14 total. 8 of those processed by Fontaine, Tran, or Washington. Average for comparable associates: 0-1 per month.
question: What evidence pattern supports opening a coordinated internal theft investigation versus treating these as independent low-level policy compliance issues?
choices: A) Insufficient evidence for coordinated investigation — each associate is below individual thresholds, the inventory variances could be receiving errors, and the LinkedIn connection is circumstantial; continue monitoring

B) Escalate the inventory variances to the distribution center first — the LP Exception Log suggests a receiving error, and without resolving that root cause, the refund patterns could be explained by legitimate customer returns of merchandise that was never properly received
C) Open an investigation into James Fontaine only — he has the highest transaction count and the inventory variance at his location is largest; the others may be coincidental

D) The prepaid card BIN batch match across two associates at different brands, combined with the deliberate sub-threshold transaction amounts ($88-$97 against a $100 policy limit), correlated inventory variances in the same SKU categories, and the prior employment overlap establish a coordinated scheme requiring formal investigation
rationale: The evidence, when synthesized across systems that individually see nothing alarming, reveals a coordinated pattern: (1) All transactions are deliberately structured just below the $100 LP-approval threshold, indicating knowledge of internal controls. (2) The prepaid Visa BIN match across Fontaine and Tran's transactions — discovered only in Slack by Jenny's manual analysis — proves the refund instruments came from the same batch of cards, not from random customers. (3) Inventory variances in the exact product categories being 'returned' confirm merchandise is disappearing. (4) The LinkedIn connection between Fontaine and Tran establishes a pre-existing relationship. The Looker dashboard shows these three associates account for 8 of 14 sub-$100 refund-without-receipt transactions company-wide. Answer A applies single-system threshold logic — no individual system triggers an alert, which is precisely how employee collusion rings operate below detection. Answer C incorrectly siloes the investigation to one associate, missing the coordinated nature. Answer D is a misdirection from the Exception Log note about 'receiving error' — the correlation between inventory loss and refund patterns across multiple brands makes a DC error implausible as a full explanation.
